analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: Backed by 15 House Republicans, the bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee on January 3, 2025 and has received no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The FairTax Act would repeal federal income taxes, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on almost everything people buy (30% when added on top of the price, the way state sales taxes work). Each family could get a monthly rebate covering the tax on purchases up to the federal poverty level, but every family member would need a Social Security number and lawful U.S. residency. The bill would also eliminate funding for the IRS and hand tax collection mostly to state governments. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and investors gain the most: income tax, capital gains tax, and estate tax on large inheritances disappear, and purchases made for investment purposes are untaxed. Businesses gain from lower payroll costs and untaxed business purchases. People below the poverty line roughly break even through the monthly rebate. [S2][S3]

how_it_helps.text: Repeals federal income taxes, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, ending tax filing and withholding for individuals and businesses. [S2][S3]
Provides every registered family a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax on purchases up to the federal poverty level, designed to offset the tax for basic living costs. [S2][S3]
Exempts purchases made for business, investment, and export purposes, so money saved and invested is not taxed at all. [S2][S3]

Eliminates IRS appropriations after fiscal year 2029 and replaces federal tax administration with an Excise Tax Bureau and a Sales Tax Bureau, with states collecting most of the sales tax for a 0.25% administration fee. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Consumers pay a 23% tax on nearly everything they buy, and because lower- and middle-income families spend most of their income while wealthy families save and invest much of theirs, the tax burden shifts toward ordinary spenders. Social Security and Medicare would be funded out of sales tax revenue instead of dedicated payroll taxes. Families without a Social Security number or lawful residency status would pay the tax but could not receive the rebate. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, especially lower- and middle-income families

drawbacks.text: A 23% tax-inclusive rate means a 30% markup on the price tag of goods and services, and only the poverty-level portion is rebated, so a middle-income family spending well above poverty pays the full rate on most of its purchases while the largest untaxed purchases go to those who can save and invest. [S2][S3]

The bill sunsets the entire sales tax if the Sixteenth Amendment, which authorizes the federal income tax, is not repealed within seven years — repeal requires ratification by 38 states, which has never come close — so the bill as written could leave the federal government with neither the income tax nor the sales tax. [S2][S3]

Rebate eligibility requires a Social Security number and lawful U.S. residency for every family member, and families must register annually and certify no member is incarcerated, or the rebate lapses. [S2][S3]
Social Security and Medicare would depend entirely on sales tax collections rather than the dedicated payroll tax, changing how those programs are financed. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real appeal — no more income tax filing, no IRS — is genuine, and the poverty-level rebate protects the very poorest. But the design shifts a large share of the tax burden from wealth to consumption: households that live on their paychecks would pay the sales tax on nearly every dollar they spend, while households that live on accumulated wealth would pay almost nothing, and the repeal of the estate tax is a direct transfer to the largest inheritances. The seven-year sunset tied to a constitutional amendment that will not be repealed adds a serious revenue-risk flaw. On balance, the costs fall more heavily on ordinary working families than the benefits reach them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got a referral to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there ever since, with no hearing, markup, or vote. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter introduced the FairTax Act of 2025 in the House on January 3, 2025, with nine original cosponsors. [S1][S5]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the committee that must act on any tax legislation. [S5]
Fourteen Republicans joined as cosponsors; no Democrat or independent has signed on. [S4]
As of the latest recorded action, the committee has taken no further step — no hearing, no markup, no vote — since the January 2025 referral. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing happened, current law stands: high-income households keep the existing income and estate tax structure (with its deductions and rates), and the tax preparation and compliance industry keeps its market. Ordinary families saw no change in either direction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the current tax system

for.name: Rep. Earl L. 'Buddy' Carter
for.role: U.S. Representative, Georgia's 1st District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FairTax Act of 2025 in the House and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: 14 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent cosponsored.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as committee chair and has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; its only recorded action to date is the January 3, 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters (the sponsor and 14 cosponsors) are House Republicans, about 7% of the 223-member Republican conference; no Democrat or independent supports the bill, and the Republican-run committee has not acted on it. [S4][S5]

industries.note: The bill eliminates income tax on wages and investment returns, ends the estate and gift tax on large inheritances, and leaves purchases made for investment purposes untaxed, while shifting the revenue burden to a sales tax on consumption that savers largely avoid. Wealthy households would keep far more; spending households would pay the tax at the register. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and abolishing the IRS eliminates the filing, software, and advisory market that tax preparation firms and accountants depend on. Their interest lies in keeping the current system that this bill would dismantle. [S2][S3]

Sellers must register, collect the tax, maintain segregated accounts, post security bonds if large, and face penalties for failures, but they receive an administration credit of at least $200 per filing month and compensation for collecting. Payroll tax relief cuts their employment costs. [S2][S3]
States with their own sales taxes can become the primary collectors of the federal tax for a 0.25% administration fee, expanding their role and revenue in tax administration. [S2][S3]
Financial intermediation services are taxed under the bill, but investment purchases and financial instruments are otherwise exempt, and sellers' collection duties come with credits. [S2][S3]

analysis.trajectory: With 15 supporters out of 435 House members, no Democratic support, and no committee action more than a year after referral, the bill is very likely to remain in committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of this Congress, as prior versions of the FairTax have.
